This process underlies autonomic dysreflexia, a syndrome of sudden uncontrolled hypertension that is repeatedly described as a life-threatening complication after injury above the sixth thoracic level [[91]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40963010) [[92]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35304427) [[93]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36381835). Experimental work has shown that thoracic excitatory spinal interneurons drive structural remodeling of sympathetic pathways after injury and thereby increase the frequency and severity of hypertensive episodes, while inhibition of these neurons reduces dysautonomia and autonomic dysreflexia [[92]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35304427). In parallel, persistent soluble tumor necrosis factor alpha signaling promotes sympathetic hyperreflexia, and delayed intrathecal blockade attenuates autonomic dysreflexia for months, supporting a causal role for inflammatory remodeling in postinjury hypertension [[94]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31754014). Clinical studies further demonstrate that common procedures such as urodynamic testing can provoke profound blood pressure surges, with systolic arterial pressure exceeding 200 millimeters of mercury in autonomically complete injuries, emphasizing that hypertension after spinal cord injury is often stimulus-evoked, severe, and arrhythmogenic rather than simply essential hypertension in a disabled population [[95]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36187786). Additional evidence suggests that pain can trigger hypertensive episodes after spinal cord injury and that interventions such as propofol or spinal cord stimulation can reduce these responses, again implicating aberrant sensory autonomic coupling in blood pressure elevation [[96]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40166966) [[97]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39238671). Beyond direct autonomic mechanisms, spinal cord injury also promotes cardiometabolic states linked to hypertension, including dyslipidemia, diabetes, adipose tissue dysfunction, and physical deconditioning; sensory plasticity in adipose-innervating pathways has been shown experimentally to disturb lipid handling after injury, offering a plausible route by which spinal cord injury may further increase chronic vascular risk [[98]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38663398) [[99]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39517327). Taken together, these studies support the interpretation that spinal cord injury may contribute to hypertension by disrupting central autonomic regulation, inducing maladaptive sympathetic plasticity and inflammatory signaling, precipitating recurrent hypertensive crises through autonomic dysreflexia, and fostering long-term metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidity.[[90]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41186949) [[91]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40963010) [[94]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31754014) [[92]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35304427) [[95]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36187786) [[98]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38663398) [[99]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39517327) [[96]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40166966) [[93]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36381835) [[97]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39238671) 

To extend this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis provides a complementary molecular view of how this pathway may relate to hypertension. There were 19 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing spinal cord injury as a pathological state that disrupts autonomic cardiovascular regulation, vascular control, immune signaling, endocrine balance, and metabolic homeostasis, thereby linking traumatic or perioperative spinal cord damage to sustained blood pressure dysregulation, episodic hypertensive responses, and increased long-term vascular risk. This enrichment profile is quantitatively notable because it captures a 19-protein disease-relevant functional module centered on mechanisms directly pertinent to hypertension, including altered sympathetic signaling, exaggerated pressor reflexes, inflammatory remodeling, and cardiometabolic disturbance, all of which are described as contributing to elevated blood pressure burden, hypertensive crises, stroke risk, and coronary artery disease in the pathway annotation. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 19 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link.

![PPI Network](imgs/13ff51a1-2176-4019-96b8-77223022ff22.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=47102B34D07428F1)

With this network-level context in place, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified during the functional enrichment analysis and consider, in a cautious manner, how they may relate to hypertension.
NOS1 is the protein in this list with the clearest and most direct mechanistic relevance to hypertension because nitric oxide is a central regulator of vascular tone, autonomic control, and renal sodium handling. Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability is a well-established contributor to increased peripheral vascular resistance, endothelial dysfunction, and sustained blood pressure elevation. Although NOS3 is classically emphasized in the vasculature, NOS1 also contributes importantly to blood pressure homeostasis through neural and renal mechanisms, including modulation of sympathetic neurotransmission and regulation of tubuloglomerular feedback and natriuresis in the kidney. Its role in neuronal nitric oxide signaling is especially relevant because neurogenic mechanisms are increasingly recognized in hypertension pathogenesis. In addition, aberrant S-nitrosylation signaling may influence redox balance and intracellular signaling pathways implicated in vascular remodeling and end-organ damage. Therefore, among the proteins listed, NOS1 appears to be the strongest candidate for a meaningful connection to hypertension pathophysiology.

A related but somewhat different line of reasoning concerns proteins involved in structural remodeling of the vascular wall. MMP12 is potentially relevant to hypertension because extracellular matrix remodeling and large-artery stiffening are major determinants of elevated systolic blood pressure and hypertensive target-organ damage. Its significant elastolytic activity is particularly notable, as degradation of elastic fiber components can reduce arterial compliance and promote vascular stiffening, a hallmark of aging-associated and inflammation-associated hypertension. Beyond direct matrix degradation, MMP12 may participate in inflammatory vascular remodeling, which contributes to resistance vessel dysfunction, altered pulse-wave propagation, and maladaptive cardiac and renal changes. Although MMP12 is not among the canonical blood pressure genes, its function aligns closely with structural mechanisms that may sustain or worsen hypertension, especially in contexts of chronic inflammation, vascular injury, or remodeling of the arterial wall.

In contrast to these more established vascular and renal mechanisms, some candidates may be relevant through signaling systems that bridge neural and cardiovascular biology. RGMA is an intriguing candidate in relation to hypertension because its biology intersects with two pathways that are highly relevant to cardiovascular disease: RHOA-ROCK signaling and bone morphogenetic protein-associated signaling. The RHOA-ROCK pathway is strongly implicated in vasoconstriction, vascular smooth muscle contractility, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular remodeling, all of which contribute to hypertension. Although the function provided here emphasizes neuronal growth cone collapse and neurite inhibition, the signaling architecture suggests a broader relevance to cytoskeletal regulation and tissue remodeling. Its additional role as a bone morphogenetic protein coreceptor is also noteworthy, as bone morphogenetic protein and transforming growth factor beta family signaling has recognized roles in vascular homeostasis, inflammation, and remodeling. Thus, RGMA may be relevant not because it is a classic hypertension effector, but because it connects neurodevelopmental guidance mechanisms with signaling modules known to influence vascular tone and structural adaptation in hypertensive disease.

This emphasis on neural organization also provides a natural transition to extracellular matrix proteins that may shape autonomic circuitry more indirectly. BCAN has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to hypertension through the central nervous system regulation of blood pressure. Because it contributes to the organization and stabilization of the neural extracellular matrix, BCAN may influence neuronal connectivity, synaptic microenvironments, and signaling within brain regions involved in autonomic cardiovascular control. Hypertension is increasingly understood to involve central neuroplastic and neuroinflammatory mechanisms, particularly within hypothalamic and brainstem circuits that regulate sympathetic outflow. Although there is no direct indication here that BCAN controls vascular function, its role in maintaining the mature nervous system extracellular environment suggests a plausible link to neurogenic components of hypertension. This makes BCAN more speculative than NOS1, but still of interest if the biological context involves central autonomic regulation.

A closely related interpretation may also apply to NCAN, which appears most plausibly connected to hypertension through neurodevelopmental and neuroregulatory mechanisms rather than direct vascular actions. By modulating neuronal adhesion, neurite growth, and extracellular matrix interactions, NCAN may influence the formation or maintenance of neural circuits that govern autonomic balance. Since sympathetic overactivity is a major driver of many forms of hypertension, proteins that shape neuronal connectivity may have indirect relevance to disease susceptibility or progression. However, compared with NOS1 or MMP12, the current functional description supports only a relatively indirect association. NCAN may therefore be best regarded as a secondary candidate whose importance would depend on whether the disease model emphasizes central nervous system remodeling, autonomic dysregulation, or extracellular matrix changes in neural tissues.

### Overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators (WP:WP5095) 

The pathway described as an overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators represents a convergent biological network that links immune activation, neurohormonal signaling, mechanical stress, cellular activation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. In this pathway, proinflammatory mediators such as cytokines and related signaling molecules promote the recruitment and activation of inflammatory and stromal cells, while profibrotic mediators such as growth factors and hormone-dependent signals stimulate fibroblast activation, myofibroblast transition, collagen synthesis, and structural remodeling of tissues. The publications provided suggest that this pathway is strongly influenced by pressure overload and by excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. In the cardiovascular setting, increased mechanical stress and inflammatory signaling activate fibroblasts and induce intracellular signaling pathways, especially mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, which enhances extracellular matrix production and tissue stiffening. In the kidney, angiotensin two and aldosterone act not only as regulators of vascular tone and salt-water balance but also as direct proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators that damage the vascular endothelium, glomerulus, and renal interstitium. Taken together, this pathway may be understood as a disease-amplifying axis in which hemodynamic stress, inflammatory mediators, and fibrotic signaling reinforce one another, potentially leading to maladaptive remodeling in the heart, vasculature, and kidney.  

This broader mechanistic framework provides a useful basis for understanding why the pathway appears closely related to hypertension. Hypertension both activates and is sustained by proinflammatory and profibrotic signaling across multiple organs. One publication shows that pressure overload increases levels of proinflammatory cytokines, profibrotic growth factors, and mechanical stimulation, which activate cardiac fibroblasts, trigger mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and promote extracellular matrix synthesis and remodeling; although initially adaptive, this fibrotic response ultimately increases myocardial stiffness and impairs ventricular function, illustrating how elevated pressure can be translated into structural heart disease in hypertensive states [[100]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36940790). A second publication demonstrates that excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system promotes systemic and glomerular capillary hypertension and, beyond its hemodynamic actions, directly drives inflammation and fibrosis through angiotensin two and aldosterone, thereby injuring the vascular endothelium and kidney tissue [[101]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969655). Taken together, these studies support a unified model in which hypertension is not simply a disorder of elevated blood pressure, but a chronic pathological condition in which neurohormonal activation, inflammatory signaling, and fibrotic remodeling interact to damage target organs. In this context, proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators may contribute to vascular dysfunction, renal injury, cardiac stiffening, and progressive end-organ remodeling, while these structural changes may in turn further worsen blood pressure regulation, thereby creating a self-perpetuating cycle of hypertensive disease.[[100]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36940790) [[101]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969655) 

Building on this disease-level interpretation, the enrichment results provide quantitative support for the relevance of this pathway to hypertension-associated biology. There were 39 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as an overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators, indicating that this disease-relevant functional module captures a substantial convergence of inflammatory signaling, neurohormonal activation, mechanical stress responses, fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix accumulation, and tissue remodeling. The enrichment of 39 proteins supports a broad and biologically coherent network rather than an isolated signaling event, which is consistent with the multisystem nature of hypertension, in which maladaptive remodeling affects the heart, vasculature, and kidney through interconnected molecular processes. In this pathway context, the coordinated presence of proinflammatory mediators, profibrotic growth signals, and pressure-sensitive intracellular pathways is quantitatively notable because it reflects a large set of proteins participating in disease amplification, where hemodynamic load and hormone-driven signaling may jointly intensify structural damage and functional decline.

To further illustrate the organization of this enriched protein set, the network representation is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 39 proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive inspection of the network topology and connectivity relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/67ab1698-8a34-4053-bcd6-4bcde209bf7f.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=991FF97B5A0F316F)

With this network context in mind, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
Among the listed proteins, VEGFA is one of the most directly relevant to hypertension because it is centrally involved in endothelial biology, vascular remodeling, and vascular tone regulation. Its receptor-mediated signaling promotes endothelial survival, migration, and angiogenesis, while also inducing NOS2/NOS3-dependent nitric oxide production, a major determinant of vasodilation and vascular homeostasis. In the context of hypertension, impaired endothelial function and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability are core pathophysiological features; therefore, molecules that regulate endothelial nitric oxide signaling and vascular integrity are highly pertinent. VEGFA also increases vascular permeability and activates PI3K-AKT, MAPK, SRC, and FAK signaling, pathways strongly linked to vascular adaptation and remodeling under hemodynamic stress. Dysregulated VEGFA activity may therefore contribute either to compensatory vascular repair or, when excessive or imbalanced, to pathological angiogenesis and endothelial dysfunction that accompany hypertensive target-organ injury.  

Extending from endothelial regulation to cardiometabolic adaptation, EPO also appears potentially relevant within this dataset. EPO stands out because several of its reported functions intersect with mechanisms relevant to hypertension and hypertensive end-organ damage, particularly in the cardiovascular and metabolic systems. Most notably, EPO inhibits apoptosis and inflammatory responses in cardiomyocytes through AKT pathway activation [[102]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30566056), suggesting a potential protective role in the myocardium under hemodynamic stress. Since chronic hypertension promotes cardiac remodeling, inflammation, and myocyte injury, this anti-apoptotic signaling is mechanistically important. In addition, its effects on hepatocyte autophagy and lipid uptake [[103]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22351773) [[104]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24187137) connect EPO to systemic metabolic regulation, which is highly relevant because metabolic dysfunction frequently coexists with hypertension and worsens vascular disease. Its endocrine role in iron homeostasis after blood loss [[105]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24880340) [[106]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30097509) [[107]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31800957) [[108]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34002695) may be less directly linked to blood pressure itself, but altered erythropoietic and iron-regulatory states can influence blood viscosity, tissue oxygenation, and cardiovascular strain. Collectively, the strongest hypertension-related implication of EPO in this dataset is its modulation of cardiomyocyte survival and inflammatory signaling, with additional relevance through metabolic and systemic homeostatic pathways.[[105]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24880340) [[106]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30097509) [[107]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31800957) [[108]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34002695) [[103]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22351773) [[102]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30566056) [[104]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24187137) 

A related remodeling-oriented perspective may also be considered for AREG. AREG is potentially relevant to hypertension because EGFR ligand signaling is strongly associated with cellular growth, proliferation, and tissue remodeling. Although the description provided here is concise, its mitogenic activity in fibroblasts is especially noteworthy in the setting of hypertension, where vascular and cardiac fibrosis are major determinants of disease progression and target-organ damage. EGFR pathway activation has been broadly implicated in vascular smooth muscle activation, fibroblast proliferation, and maladaptive remodeling, all of which contribute to increased vascular stiffness and elevated peripheral resistance. Thus, AREG may represent a plausible mediator of hypertensive remodeling, particularly through autocrine and paracrine growth-promoting effects in stromal and mesenchymal cell populations.  

In parallel with growth factor-driven remodeling, inflammatory cytokine signaling may provide another layer of relevance. IL17C is relevant to hypertension because chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to vascular dysfunction, endothelial injury, and hypertensive end-organ damage. The function described here emphasizes activation of NF-kappa-B and MAPK pathways and synergy with TNF and IL1B, which are canonical inflammatory axes implicated in vascular inflammation and remodeling. Although IL17C is primarily characterized as an epithelial cytokine, its ability to amplify inflammatory programs suggests a plausible role in systemic inflammatory states that predispose to or exacerbate hypertension. The note that enhanced IL17C/IL17RE signaling may increase susceptibility to autoimmune disease further strengthens its relevance, as immune dysregulation and cytokine-driven inflammation are increasingly linked to resistant and organ-damaging forms of hypertension.  

By contrast, IL19 may be interpreted somewhat differently, as its reported functions suggest a potentially counter-regulatory role. IL19 is notable because it combines anti-inflammatory and proangiogenic properties, both of which may be meaningful in hypertension. Its capacity to polarize immunity toward a Th2 phenotype and suppress IFN-gamma [[109]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16365913) suggests a counter-regulatory role against pro-inflammatory immune activation, a known driver of endothelial dysfunction and vascular injury in hypertension. In addition, proangiogenic signaling and activation of JAK-STAT, especially STAT3 [[110]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11564763), may influence vascular adaptation and tissue repair. Depending on context, such effects could be beneficial by limiting inflammatory vascular damage, although persistent STAT3-associated signaling can also participate in remodeling responses. Therefore, IL19 may be interpreted as a potentially protective immunoregulatory cytokine within hypertensive disease biology, particularly where inflammation contributes to progression.[[111]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34932373) [[109]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16365913) [[112]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12351624) [[110]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11564763) 

Another potentially relevant inflammatory component is CCL5-related signaling, although its connection appears somewhat more indirect. CCL5-related signaling may have a meaningful, albeit somewhat indirect, connection to hypertension through inflammatory chemokine biology and calcium-dependent signal transduction. The described receptor function includes calcium mobilization and activation of PI3K-AKT and MAP kinase pathways, which are broadly relevant to vascular cell activation and inflammatory responses. In addition, the reported connection to insulin secretion suggests a link to metabolic regulation, and metabolic dysfunction is a major comorbidity that promotes hypertension. While the annotation provided here emphasizes neuronal and pancreatic effects rather than direct vascular actions, chemokine pathways such as CCL5 are frequently implicated in leukocyte recruitment and vascular inflammation, making this axis potentially relevant to hypertensive vascular injury and metabolic-cardiovascular crosstalk.  

Finally, IL12B may add a complementary perspective centered on oxidative stress control and cellular stress responses. Although IL12B is not as directly connected to blood pressure regulation as VEGFA or EPO, the functions listed suggest relevance to hypertension through oxidative stress, innate immunity, and autophagy. Oxidative stress and defective proteostasis are well-established contributors to endothelial dysfunction, vascular stiffness, and hypertensive organ injury. In particular, activation of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway and regulation of inflammatory signaling [[113]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916398) [[114]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34374750) may influence how vascular and immune cells respond to chronic stress. Because hypertension is increasingly understood as a disorder involving immune activation and redox imbalance, proteins that coordinate autophagy and antioxidant defense may have mechanistic importance, especially in the progression of vascular and renal damage.[[113]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916398) [[114]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34374750)

### glycosaminoglycan binding (GO:0005539) 

Glycosaminoglycan binding denotes the selective physical interaction of proteins with glycosaminoglycans, a class of linear, highly charged polysaccharides enriched in amino sugars and commonly attached to proteoglycan core proteins or present as free extracellular matrix polymers such as hyaluronan. In vascular and cardiovascular tissues, glycosaminoglycans are major structural and signaling components of the extracellular matrix, endothelial surface layer, interstitium, and basement membrane. Through their dense negative charge and variable sulfation patterns, they bind growth factors, chemokines, cytokines, adhesion molecules, lipoproteins, and matrix-remodeling enzymes, thereby controlling ligand retention, concentration gradients, receptor presentation, and cell migration. Heparan sulfate-bearing proteoglycans such as syndecans and perlecan are particularly important because they organize inflammatory and fibrotic signaling at the cell surface, regulate smooth muscle cell behavior, and influence endothelial barrier properties. Hyaluronan, another glycosaminoglycan, contributes to endothelial glycocalyx integrity and vascular homeostasis, and its loss or remodeling is linked to endothelial dysfunction. Beyond these more classical extracellular matrix functions, glycosaminoglycans also participate in sodium buffering within the skin interstitium, where negatively charged glycosaminoglycan networks can store sodium in an osmotically less active form and thereby influence immune sensing, lymphatic adaptation, and systemic blood pressure regulation. Taken together, glycosaminoglycan binding may be viewed not as a narrow biochemical event, but as a broader organizing principle linking extracellular matrix composition to inflammation, vascular remodeling, fibrosis, salt handling, and tissue stiffness.

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that glycosaminoglycan binding is mechanistically relevant to hypertension because glycosaminoglycan-interacting molecules appear to regulate several core processes that drive elevated blood pressure and hypertensive organ injury, including vascular inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial dysfunction, fibrosis, and tissue sodium handling. A major theme is that glycosaminoglycan-rich proteoglycans act as signaling scaffolds in cardiovascular remodeling. The review on syndecans shows that syndecan family members, through their extracellular heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycan chains, bind collagens, growth factors, cytokines, and immune cell adhesion proteins, thereby promoting profibrotic signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and cardiac stiffness in settings that include hypertension and pressure overload, linking glycosaminoglycan binding directly to hypertensive cardiac fibrosis and adverse remodeling [[115]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27411689). Consistent with this concept, perlecan heparan sulfate deficiency attenuated hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension by impairing fibroblast growth factor two and fibroblast growth factor receptor one complex formation, reducing pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell proliferation, and altering cell-matrix interactions, suggesting that heparan sulfate-dependent ligand binding can amplify vascular remodeling in hypertensive disease [[116]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25952902). 

This remodeling-centered framework also connects naturally to inflammation, which is widely recognized as an important component of hypertension. Glycosaminoglycan binding also shapes inflammatory cell recruitment, an established contributor to hypertension. Matrix metalloproteinase processing enhanced the glycosaminoglycan binding of chemokine ligand sixteen and activated monocyte-attracting chemokines, supporting the idea that altered chemokine retention within glycosaminoglycan-rich matrices can intensify leukocyte recruitment and sustain vascular inflammation [[117]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22147696). This observation appears relevant to hypertension because angiotensin two-induced hypertension was shown to depend on vascular smooth muscle cell inflammatory signaling and immune cell infiltration, with resolvin E one reducing chemokine ligand five expression, macrophage infiltration, T cell infiltration, vascular smooth muscle cell phenotypic switching, fibrosis, and blood pressure, thereby highlighting inflammatory retention and trafficking pathways that may plausibly be modulated by glycosaminoglycan interactions within the vessel wall [[118]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37800344). 

A second major connection concerns salt-sensitive blood pressure regulation, which extends the relevance of glycosaminoglycans beyond local vascular signaling. The review of the skin lymphatic system emphasizes that skin glycosaminoglycans bind and store sodium, creating local hypertonicity that activates macrophage tonicity-responsive enhancer binding protein and vascular endothelial growth factor C-dependent lymphatic adaptation; disruption of this buffering and clearance axis is implicated in salt-sensitive hypertension [[119]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33350284). Human evidence from primary aldosteronism further supports this tissue sodium concept, showing altered skin electrolyte and water handling together with activation of tonicity-responsive enhancer binding protein and normalization after adrenalectomy, which is compatible with a glycosaminoglycan-rich interstitial compartment participating in blood pressure regulation [[120]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39355924). 

In parallel with these interstitial mechanisms, endothelial glycosaminoglycans may also be pertinent to hypertensive vascular dysfunction. Hyaluronan is a key component of the endothelial glycocalyx, and its loss has been linked to endothelial dysfunction in hypertension, while elevated circulating hyaluronan in pulmonary hypertension suggests active matrix remodeling and glycocalyx disturbance in hypertensive vascular disease [[121]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20730694) [[122]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23629694). Finally, genetic and proteolytic remodeling of the extracellular matrix provides an additional link between this pathway and hypertension: matrix metalloproteinase seven promoter variation increased hypertension risk and circulating matrix metalloproteinase seven, consistent with enhanced extracellular matrix turnover that can modify glycosaminoglycan-associated ligand presentation and vascular structure [[123]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31656093). Taken together, the evidence supports a model in which glycosaminoglycan binding may regulate how cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and sodium are retained and sensed within cardiovascular and interstitial tissues, thereby influencing vascular tone, immune infiltration, fibrosis, endothelial integrity, and long-term hypertensive remodeling.[[115]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27411689) [[116]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25952902) [[117]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22147696) [[118]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37800344) [[119]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33350284) [[120]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39355924) [[121]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20730694) [[122]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23629694) [[123]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31656093) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment result provides a quantitative indication that this functional category may be relevant in hypertension. There were 34 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of glycosaminoglycan binding, indicating a substantial concentration of disease-relevant molecules within an extracellular matrix and vascular regulatory function that is highly pertinent to blood pressure control. This enrichment is biologically notable because glycosaminoglycan binding governs the selective interaction of proteins with highly charged polysaccharides that shape endothelial surface properties, extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory signaling, fibrotic remodeling, and sodium storage, all of which are quantitatively and mechanistically linked to hypertension pathogenesis. In vascular tissues, glycosaminoglycans regulate the local retention and presentation of growth factors, chemokines, cytokines, adhesion molecules, lipoproteins, and matrix-remodeling enzymes, thereby influencing multiple pathological dimensions at once, including endothelial dysfunction, smooth muscle cell activation, interstitial stiffening, and immune-associated salt handling. The identification of 34 proteins in this pathway therefore supports the interpretation that hypertension may involve not only hemodynamic imbalance, but also coordinated alterations in extracellular matrix signaling and tissue microenvironmental control.

To further contextualize these 34 proteins, the network view below illustrates their degree of interconnection. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 34 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=ED956D756375093C).

![PPI Network](imgs/71a8e5f2-f776-4348-9e79-8994f027e47d.png)

With this network context in mind, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins that may be of particular interest. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CFH stands out because dysregulated complement activation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to vascular inflammation, endothelial injury, and renal microvascular damage, all of which are highly relevant to hypertension. By restraining alternative pathway amplification at host surfaces, CFH protects the endothelium from excessive complement-mediated injury. In the context of hypertension, especially forms associated with chronic kidney disease, vascular dysfunction, or inflammatory endothelial stress, impaired complement control could exacerbate vascular remodeling and renal damage, thereby promoting blood pressure elevation. Its additional ability to influence leukocyte-pathogen and leukocyte-surface interactions further links CFH to inflammatory vascular responses that may worsen hypertensive end-organ injury.

A closely related vascular theme is represented by growth factor signaling that regulates endothelial homeostasis. VEGFA-related signaling is one of the most directly relevant pathways to hypertension because it governs endothelial integrity, microvascular density, vascular permeability, and nitric oxide bioavailability. Endothelial nitric oxide is a central determinant of vascular tone; thus, proteins that mediate VEGFA-dependent nitric oxide synthase activation can influence vasodilation and peripheral resistance. Disturbance of VEGFA signaling is also strongly linked to capillary rarefaction and endothelial dysfunction, both established mechanisms in hypertension. Moreover, excessive or maladaptive VEGFA activity may contribute to vascular leakage and remodeling, whereas insufficient signaling may impair endothelial survival and nitric oxide generation. Accordingly, this pathway appears highly pertinent to both primary hypertension and hypertensive vascular complications.

From endothelial regulation, the discussion transitions naturally to profibrotic signaling and structural remodeling. TGFBR2 is highly relevant to hypertension because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major driver of vascular remodeling, fibrosis, extracellular matrix accumulation, and chronic renal injury. These processes increase arterial stiffness and impair vascular compliance, two hallmarks of sustained hypertension. In the kidney, excessive transforming growth factor beta signaling promotes fibrotic remodeling that can worsen sodium handling and renal perfusion, thereby contributing to blood pressure elevation and target-organ damage. Its role in mesenchymal cell behavior and wound-healing programs also links TGFBR2 to hypertensive remodeling of the vessel wall and myocardium. Thus, TGFBR2 may represent a mechanistically important node connecting inflammation, fibrosis, and structural vascular disease in hypertension.[[124]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) 

Another protein that may intersect with both vascular protection and inflammatory signaling is FSTL1. FSTL1 is notable because it integrates vascular, inflammatory, and cardioprotective signaling, all of which are central to hypertension pathophysiology. Its ability to promote endothelial survival and angiogenic network formation suggests a potentially protective role against endothelial dysfunction and microvascular rarefaction. In addition, support of cardiac myocyte survival may be relevant in hypertensive heart disease, where chronic pressure overload induces myocardial stress and remodeling. Because FSTL1 can also signal through immune-related receptors such as toll-like receptor four, it may participate in the inflammatory component of hypertension. Overall, FSTL1 appears to lie at the intersection of vascular repair, inflammation, and cardiac adaptation, making it particularly relevant to hypertensive target-organ responses.[[125]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19595790) [[126]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21826198) [[127]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20054002) 

Extending this theme of coordinated inflammation and vascular remodeling, MDK emerges as another plausible candidate. MDK is one of the strongest candidates for a connection to hypertension because it links inflammation, vascular growth, endothelial signaling, and tissue remodeling. It recruits neutrophils and macrophages to inflammatory sites, induces chemokine expression, and modulates regenerative responses after tissue injury, features that are highly compatible with the chronic low-grade inflammatory milieu observed in hypertension. Importantly, MDK can stimulate VEGFA expression and nitric oxide synthase activation during vascular remodeling, indicating a direct role in endothelial adaptation and vascular tone regulation. At the same time, its pro-migratory and pro-survival effects on smooth muscle and other stromal cells may favor maladaptive vascular remodeling if dysregulated. These combined properties suggest that MDK could contribute both to compensatory vascular repair and to the progression of hypertensive vascular disease.[[128]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [[129]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [[130]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [[131]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [[132]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [[133]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [[134]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [[135]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [[136]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [[137]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

A conceptually related growth factor is PTN, which may be relevant through somewhat more indirect vascular mechanisms. PTN is relevant to hypertension primarily through its effects on endothelial migration, cell survival, and phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B signaling, which are central to vascular adaptation and remodeling. Its interaction with endothelial integrin complexes and promotion of endothelial motility suggest a role in vascular repair responses. In addition, PTN participates in hematopoietic and regenerative processes, which may influence inflammatory and vascular homeostasis in hypertensive states. Because hypertension is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular wall signaling, and structural remodeling, a growth factor such as PTN that coordinates these processes is of considerable interest. Although the evidence here is more indirect than for TGFBR2 or VEGFA-related pathways, PTN plausibly contributes to the vascular remodeling axis of hypertension.[[138]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11414790) [[139]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15121180) [[140]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16619002) [[141]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17121547) [[142]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19442624) [[143]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21791434) [[144]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25000129) [[145]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27445335) [[146]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28657144) [[147]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30497772) 

The next group of proteins further emphasizes the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive remodeling. SFRP1 is particularly interesting in hypertension because Wnt and beta-catenin signaling has been implicated in vascular remodeling, fibrosis, and renal injury. By antagonizing Wnt signaling and suppressing vascular cell proliferation, SFRP1 could influence arterial wall thickening and maladaptive remodeling, both of which contribute to increased peripheral resistance. Its reported vascular antiproliferative activity makes it especially relevant to the structural component of hypertension. At the same time, the observation that it can induce angiogenic responses suggests context-dependent effects on vascular homeostasis. Thus, SFRP1 may act as a regulator of the balance between pathological remodeling and adaptive vascular repair in hypertensive disease.

In a similar extracellular matrix context, THBS2 may be relevant through effects on angiogenesis and microvascular structure. THBS2 is relevant because antiangiogenic extracellular matrix regulators can contribute to microvascular rarefaction, a well-established feature of hypertension. Reduced microvascular density increases peripheral vascular resistance and impairs tissue perfusion, thereby promoting sustained blood pressure elevation and end-organ ischemia. Through its effects on cell-matrix interactions and angiogenesis inhibition, THBS2 may also participate in vascular stiffening and remodeling. Its functional profile therefore aligns with mechanisms that connect extracellular matrix remodeling and impaired angiogenic capacity to hypertensive vascular disease.

Another matrix-associated candidate is SMOC2, which may influence endothelial behavior and vessel wall adaptation. SMOC2 stands out as a matrix-associated regulator of endothelial behavior, making it potentially relevant to the vascular remodeling that accompanies hypertension. By promoting matrix assembly and endothelial proliferation and migration, SMOC2 may influence vessel wall structure, angiogenic adaptation, and endothelial repair. In hypertension, such processes can be either beneficial, by supporting vascular maintenance, or pathogenic, by facilitating maladaptive remodeling and altered extracellular matrix composition. Its combined effects on matrix biology and angiogenesis therefore make SMOC2 a plausible contributor to hypertensive vascular changes.

This matrix-centered perspective also extends to ligand clearance and hyaluronan turnover. STAB2 is of interest in hypertension because it links extracellular matrix turnover, clearance of inflammatory or damage-associated ligands, and hyaluronan handling. Hyaluronan accumulation and altered matrix turnover are increasingly associated with vascular stiffness, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammatory remodeling, all of which are central to hypertension. Its role in scavenging advanced glycation end products is also notable, as these molecules promote vascular stiffening and oxidative stress, especially in metabolic disease-associated hypertension. Furthermore, efficient clearance of apoptotic cells may limit persistent inflammation, whereas dysfunction in this process could aggravate vascular injury. STAB2 therefore represents a plausible mediator of matrix-driven and inflammation-associated hypertensive pathology.

Within the same broad extracellular matrix environment, LAYN may also merit consideration. Although the functional annotation is brief, LAYN is potentially relevant to hypertension because hyaluronan-rich extracellular matrix environments influence vascular stiffness, endothelial activation, and inflammatory cell behavior. Receptors that sense or bind hyaluronate can modulate cell adhesion, migration, and tissue remodeling, processes that are highly pertinent to hypertensive vascular injury. Given the established importance of extracellular matrix remodeling in arterial stiffening and end-organ damage, LAYN may warrant attention as a matrix-interacting molecule with possible roles in vascular inflammation or remodeling.

Finally, FGFBP1 provides an additional link to fibroblast growth factor-mediated vascular responses. FGFBP1 is relevant because fibroblast growth factor signaling is strongly linked to vascular growth, endothelial activation, and smooth muscle biology. Its ability to promote angiogenesis and mitogenic signaling suggests a role in vascular remodeling, which is a key structural component of hypertension. Through interaction with integrins and fibroblast growth factor receptors, FGFBP1 may influence endothelial repair, vessel wall growth, and possibly pathological neovascular responses. While not as directly tied to blood pressure regulation as VEGFA or transforming growth factor beta signaling, FGFBP1 could contribute to the remodeling and adaptive vascular responses that shape hypertensive disease progression.[[148]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [[149]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [[150]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [[151]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [[152]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [[153]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [[154]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879)

### Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695) 

Neutrophil degranulation is a core effector program of innate immunity in which activated neutrophils rapidly mobilize and release the contents of distinct intracellular granule compartments into the extracellular space or onto the cell surface. These granules contain proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, matrix-remodeling enzymes, adhesion-related molecules, and inflammatory mediators. Through this process, neutrophils can eliminate pathogens, amplify leukocyte recruitment, remodel extracellular matrix, alter endothelial barrier properties, and shape tissue repair. The biological consequences of neutrophil degranulation depend on the intensity, timing, and tissue context of release. Controlled degranulation contributes to host defense and resolution of injury, whereas excessive or chronic degranulation promotes oxidative stress, proteolytic tissue damage, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, and maladaptive vascular remodeling. The cited literature highlights representative granule products such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin, all of which can influence vascular tone, nitric oxide bioavailability, extracellular matrix integrity, and inflammatory signaling. In cardiovascular and inflammatory disorders, neutrophil degranulation is increasingly viewed not merely as a marker of immune activation but as a mechanistically relevant contributor to organ injury and remodeling.

Against this biological background, the collected publications support a substantive, although still context-dependent, link between neutrophil degranulation and hypertension by indicating that neutrophil activation, granule release, and closely related extracellular trap formation participate in vascular injury, endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory amplification, and tissue remodeling that may sustain elevated blood pressure and hypertensive organ damage. Direct evidence comes from pulmonary vascular disease models, where inhibition of neutrophil activation reduced lung myeloperoxidase activity, used as an index of neutrophil degranulation, and prevented acute pulmonary artery hypertension after protamine exposure, suggesting that neutrophil degranulation can occur upstream of pressure elevation in the pulmonary circulation. Consistently, transcriptomic analysis in pulmonary arterial hypertension identified enrichment of neutrophil degranulation among disease-associated pathways, and an experimental rat study of monocrotaline-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension showed increased secretory degranulation early in disease and progressive myeloperoxidase release with oxidant stress during later stages, supporting a possible role in pulmonary vascular remodeling and progression. Evidence also extends to systemic hypertension. A large proteomic risk prediction study for incident hypertension identified neutrophil degranulation as one of the principal enriched biological pathways, suggesting that this pathway may be active before or during the transition to overt disease. Clinical observations further show that inflammatory cell signatures related to neutrophils are heightened in specific hypertensive phenotypes, as patients with non-dipping hypertension displayed elevated neutrophil-related inflammatory ratios, while another study demonstrated altered neutrophil subpopulations in arterial hypertension with fewer cytoplasmic granules together with increased reactive oxygen species production, a pattern compatible with prior or ongoing degranulation. Mechanistically, the literature indicates several routes through which degranulation may promote hypertension: released proteases and oxidant enzymes can damage the endothelium, reduce nitric oxide signaling, increase vascular stiffness, and remodel extracellular matrix; myeloperoxidase-driven oxidant chemistry can intensify halogenating stress; and degranulation is closely coupled to extracellular trap formation, which has been reviewed as a contributor to hypertension and target-organ injury. Experimental work presented in a hypertension model further showed that inability to efficiently form extracellular traps attenuated angiotensin-induced hypertension and improved vascular reactivity, while hypertensive stretch augmented extracellular trap formation, thereby linking neutrophil effector activation to vascular dysfunction. Additional support comes from pregnancy-induced hypertension, in which circulating neutrophil elastase was elevated and proposed to contribute to vascular lesions. Taken together, these studies suggest that neutrophil degranulation is not only an inflammatory correlate of hypertension but also a plausible pathogenic mechanism connecting immune activation to endothelial injury, oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, abnormal vascular reactivity, and progression of both pulmonary and systemic hypertensive disease.[[155]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8103132) [[156]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41706425) [[157]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41717706) [[158]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39686847) [[159]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37165667) [[160]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2775697) [[161]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41016334) [[162]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33811902) 

This literature-based interpretation is further supported by the pathway enrichment result. There were 67 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of neutrophil degranulation, indicating a substantial convergence of hypertension-related molecular signals on an innate immune effector process that governs protease release, oxidant generation, extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial barrier regulation, and inflammatory amplification. The size of this enriched protein set, comprising 67 proteins, supports the interpretation that neutrophil degranulation is not a marginal finding but a quantitatively prominent functional theme in hypertension, consistent with the concept that excessive granule cargo release can contribute to oxidative stress, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, vascular injury, thrombogenicity, and maladaptive remodeling of the vessel wall. In this context, representative granule-associated mediators described for this pathway, including myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin, provide biologically plausible links between immune activation and the hemodynamic, endothelial, and structural abnormalities that characterize hypertension.

To place these 67 proteins into a systems-level context, the interaction network is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 67 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for further inspection of network connectivity and functional relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/4416d2a7-b42b-492d-a728-2d23fa8a192a.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=B158EC47301D9C15)

Building on this network-level overview, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help clarify how this pathway could intersect with hypertension-related biology. We will introduce them in detail in the following.

CD14 is among the most compelling hypertension-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface between innate immune sensing, vascular inflammation, and lipid-driven inflammatory signaling. Chronic low-grade inflammation is now recognized as a central contributor to hypertension, particularly through endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and enhanced cytokine production. By promoting Toll-like receptor four and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-dependent inflammatory activation in response to lipopolysaccharide, and potentially mediating inflammatory responses to modified low-density lipoprotein, CD14 may contribute to the sterile and microbial inflammatory signals that exacerbate vascular stiffness and impair vasodilatory homeostasis. These functions are especially relevant in hypertension associated with metabolic dysfunction, obesity, or vascular injury, where innate immune activation amplifies arterial inflammation and target-organ damage.[[163]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [[164]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [[165]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [[166]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

A closely related theme is extracellular matrix signaling and fibrotic remodeling, which brings attention to integrin subunit alpha V. ITGAV stands out because of its direct connection to extracellular matrix signaling, vascular remodeling, and transforming growth factor beta activation, all of which are highly relevant to hypertension pathogenesis. Transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major driver of vascular fibrosis, arterial stiffening, and renal injury, which are hallmarks of chronic hypertension and hypertensive end-organ damage. Through its role in activating latent transforming growth factor beta one, ITGAV-containing integrins may facilitate profibrotic signaling in the vasculature and kidney. In addition, alpha-V integrins participate in angiogenesis, endothelial-matrix interactions, and inflammatory signaling, suggesting that dysregulation of ITGAV could influence both structural and signaling components of elevated blood pressure. This makes ITGAV particularly relevant to mechanisms linking matrix remodeling with persistent increases in vascular resistance.[[167]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [[168]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [[169]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [[170]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [[171]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

In parallel with matrix remodeling, maintenance of endothelial structure is also likely to be important in this pathway context. PTPRB is highly relevant to hypertension because endothelial integrity is fundamental to vascular tone regulation, barrier function, and resistance vessel remodeling. Hypertension is strongly associated with endothelial dysfunction, including altered junctional stability, increased permeability, and impaired nitric oxide-dependent signaling. A protein that helps maintain endothelial polarity, lumen formation, and cell-cell junction organization could plausibly influence vascular responsiveness and microvascular health. Dysfunction in these processes may promote vascular rarefaction, inflammation, and stiffness, thereby contributing to increased peripheral resistance and hypertensive target-organ injury. Thus, PTPRB is notable as a vascular homeostasis regulator with mechanistic relevance to blood pressure control.[[172]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20332120) [[173]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9220534) [[174]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806444) [[175]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27466317) [[176]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33972531) 

Beyond endothelial regulation, metabolic inflammation may offer another route through which this pathway intersects with hypertension. FABP5 is of particular interest in hypertension because it connects lipid handling, inflammatory signaling, and transcriptional control. Hypertension frequently coexists with obesity, insulin resistance, and altered fatty acid metabolism, and these metabolic disturbances can drive vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. FABP5-mediated transport of fatty acids and retinoic acid to nuclear receptors may reshape gene programs involved in vascular cell survival, inflammation, and remodeling. Its reported role in nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and prostaglandin E2 biosynthesis further strengthens its relevance, as inflammatory lipid mediators contribute to vascular dysfunction and renal sodium-handling abnormalities. FABP5 may therefore represent a mechanistic bridge between metabolic inflammation and hypertensive vascular disease.[[177]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12540600) [[178]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8608126) [[179]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17512406) [[180]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29440395) [[181]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29531087) 

Immune restraint mechanisms may be equally informative, particularly where persistent inflammation sustains vascular injury. LAIR1 is relevant to hypertension because immune dysregulation is increasingly recognized as a driver of blood pressure elevation and end-organ damage. T cells, innate immune cells, and inflammatory cytokines contribute to vascular dysfunction, renal inflammation, and fibrosis in experimental and human hypertension. As a broad inhibitory checkpoint receptor, LAIR1 may restrain these pathogenic immune responses by limiting calcium signaling, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation, and inflammatory cytokine output. Reduced inhibitory signaling through pathways such as LAIR1 could therefore favor chronic vascular inflammation and hypertensive remodeling, whereas preserved LAIR1 activity may be protective. Its importance lies less in direct hemodynamic control and more in modulation of the inflammatory milieu that sustains hypertension.[[182]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12874256) [[183]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12893283) [[184]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16339535) 

A similar immunoregulatory perspective applies to CD300A, which may act as another brake on excessive innate immune activation. CD300A is noteworthy because it suppresses innate immune activation, particularly myeloid differentiation primary response eighty-eight-dependent Toll-like receptor signaling, a pathway with broad relevance to vascular inflammation and hypertension. Excessive Toll-like receptor-driven cytokine production can impair endothelial function, enhance oxidative stress, and promote vascular remodeling. By acting as a brake on these pathways, CD300A may influence the intensity of inflammatory responses that contribute to elevated blood pressure. Its role in mast cell regulation is also potentially relevant, as mast cell-derived mediators can affect vascular permeability, fibrosis, and local inflammatory tone. Overall, CD300A emerges as a plausible protective modulator in hypertension-associated immune activation.[[182]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12874256) [[183]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12893283) [[184]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16339535) 

In addition to these inhibitory immune receptors, interferon-associated and matrix-regulatory proteins may further broaden the inflammatory context of this pathway. BST2 is not a classic hypertension gene, but it is potentially relevant because it links interferon signaling, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activity, matrix remodeling, and cell surface protease regulation. Interferon-driven immune activation and chronic inflammatory signaling can contribute to endothelial dysfunction and vascular injury, especially in inflammatory or infection-associated cardiovascular states. The reported inhibition of matrix metalloproteinase fourteen and matrix metalloproteinase fifteen-related pathways is also notable, since matrix metalloproteinases influence extracellular matrix turnover, vascular remodeling, and arterial stiffness. BST2 may therefore be most relevant in secondary or inflammation-associated hypertension, where persistent immune activation and altered matrix regulation contribute to vascular pathology.[[185]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [[186]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [[187]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [[188]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [[189]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [[190]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [[191]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [[192]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [[193]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [[194]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [[195]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [[196]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [[197]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [[198]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

Another potentially relevant inflammatory mechanism involves nucleic acid sensing and mitochondrial stress. RNASET2 is of interest for hypertension primarily through its role in innate immune activation and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid handling. Toll-like receptor seven and Toll-like receptor eight-linked inflammatory pathways can amplify cytokine production and contribute to vascular and renal inflammation. In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction and release of mitochondrial nucleic acids are increasingly implicated in sterile inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial injury, all of which are relevant to hypertension. By controlling both microbial and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid processing, RNASET2 could influence the generation of immunostimulatory ligands that shape chronic inflammatory states. This makes it a plausible contributor to hypertension in contexts where innate immune activation and mitochondrial stress are prominent.[[199]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [[200]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [[201]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [[202]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [[203]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

Lipid trafficking provides an additional angle from which hypertension-related vascular injury may be considered. NPC2 is potentially relevant to hypertension because disturbed cholesterol trafficking and sterol homeostasis can contribute to vascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and atherosclerotic remodeling, all of which worsen arterial stiffness and cardiovascular risk in hypertensive individuals. Although NPC2 is more directly linked to lysosomal lipid transport than to blood pressure regulation itself, altered intracellular cholesterol handling can affect membrane composition, signaling platforms, and inflammatory responses in vascular and immune cells. Its role is therefore most meaningful in the broader context of cardiometabolic hypertension, where dyslipidemia and vascular injury coexist.[[204]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [[205]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [[206]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [[207]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

Related to this metabolic perspective, peroxisomal lipid oxidation may also influence vascular and inflammatory homeostasis. ACAA1 is relevant to hypertension because peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation is closely linked to systemic metabolic health, oxidative balance, and lipid-derived signaling. Impaired fatty acid catabolism can promote accumulation of bioactive lipid species that contribute to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and insulin resistance, all of which are recognized contributors to hypertension. Although the connection is indirect, ACAA1 may be particularly important in metabolic forms of hypertension where altered lipid oxidation and redox stress influence vascular tone and organ injury.[[208]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11734571) [[209]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2882519) 

Shifting from metabolism to structural remodeling, extracellular matrix composition remains another plausible contributor to elevated vascular resistance. CANT1 is noteworthy because proteoglycan synthesis is a key determinant of extracellular matrix composition and vascular wall structure. In hypertension, remodeling of the vascular extracellular matrix contributes to increased stiffness, reduced compliance, and altered mechanotransduction. A protein involved in proteoglycan biosynthesis could therefore influence arterial wall properties and susceptibility to hypertensive remodeling. While the link is less direct than for inflammatory or endothelial regulators, CANT1 may have relevance to the structural component of hypertension pathogenesis.

Finally, protein folding stress and metabolic dysfunction may offer one more mechanistic layer relevant to vascular disease. TXNDC5 may be relevant to hypertension through mechanisms involving endoplasmic reticulum stress, protein folding homeostasis, and metabolic dysfunction. Endoplasmic reticulum stress is increasingly implicated in endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and impaired insulin signaling, each of which can contribute to hypertension. As a protein disulfide isomerase, TXNDC5 may affect the maturation of secreted and membrane proteins involved in vascular signaling or inflammatory responses. Its ability to reduce insulin disulfide bonds also suggests a potential connection to insulin resistance, a common comorbidity that promotes hypertensive cardiovascular disease.[[210]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12930873) [[211]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971039)

### Signaling by Interleukins (REAC:R-HSA-449147) 

Signaling by interleukins comprises a broad cytokine communication network that coordinates innate immunity, adaptive immunity, tissue homeostasis, vascular responses, and repair. Interleukins are secreted predominantly by leukocytes, but also by endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, epithelial cells, and tissue-resident macrophages, and they act through cognate receptors that activate intracellular cascades such as janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and inflammasome-associated pathways. Depending on the ligand, receptor context, and target cell, interleukin signaling can promote leukocyte recruitment, differentiation of T helper cell subsets, endothelial activation, oxidative stress, smooth muscle migration and proliferation, barrier dysfunction, and cytokine amplification loops. In cardiovascular disease, this pathway is especially important because it links environmental and hemodynamic stressors, including excess dietary salt, hypoxia, infection, and sleep-disordered breathing, to vascular remodeling, neuroimmune activation, and end-organ injury. The publications provided highlight several interleukin-centered modules relevant to hypertension, including interleukin seventeen signaling from meningeal or gut-derived T cells, interleukin six signaling through glycoprotein one hundred thirty and soluble interleukin six receptor-dependent trans-signaling, interleukin one beta generation through inflammasome activation, and interleukin fifteen deficiency associated with impaired natural killer cell homeostasis. Collectively, these studies position interleukin signaling as a mechanistic bridge between immune dysregulation and the vascular, pulmonary, cerebral, and behavioral complications of hypertension.  

Against this biological background, the collected studies further suggest that signaling by interleukins is not merely a correlate of hypertension but may function as a mechanistic driver of disease initiation, vascular remodeling, and organ damage across systemic and pulmonary forms of hypertension. In salt-sensitive and neurogenic hypertension, excess salt and related inflammatory cues promote T cell polarization toward interleukin seventeen-producing phenotypes, and this cytokine appears to mediate both blood pressure elevation and target-organ injury. In obstructive sleep apnea-induced hypertension, interleukin seventeen neutralization reduced blood pressure and reversed gut and brain inflammation, supporting a causal role for the interleukin seventeen axis in hypertensive neuroimmune dysfunction [[212]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37260032), while in salt-sensitive hypertension, meningeal T cell-derived interleukin seventeen acted on brain border-associated macrophages to cause neurovascular dysfunction and cognitive impairment independent of the degree of blood pressure elevation, suggesting that interleukin signaling may also contribute directly to hypertensive complications [[213]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38049579). A complementary line of evidence implicates interleukin six as a central mediator of immune and vascular remodeling responses. Single-cell transcriptomics in a salt-sensitive hypertension model showed that a high-salt diet increased interleukin six receptor, janus kinase one, and signal transducer and activator of transcription three pathway activity in intestinal B cells and T follicular helper-like cells, suggesting that gut immune activation may represent an upstream component of hypertension pathogenesis [[214]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40670501). In pulmonary hypertension, multiple studies converged on pathogenic interleukin six signaling: glycoprotein one hundred thirty deletion in cluster of differentiation four-positive T cells ameliorated hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension and suppressed signal transducer and activator of transcription three activation and T helper seventeen expansion, indicating that interleukin six signaling in helper T cells may drive disease [[215]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38602915); soluble interleukin six receptor-dependent trans-signaling promoted pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cell migration and chronic hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension, identifying a specific pro-inflammatory interleukin six signaling mode linked to vascular remodeling [[216]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29767573); and endothelial studies showed that exaggerated interleukin six signaling sustains endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition-like responses and couples oxidative stress to smooth muscle proliferation, further supporting a direct vascular role for this pathway [[217]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32813135) [[218]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41177181). Interleukin one beta also emerges as an important effector downstream of danger sensing and inflammasome activation. Platelet mitochondrial dysfunction in pulmonary arterial hypertension activated the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor family pyrin domain containing three inflammasome and increased interleukin one beta release, which induced endothelial dysfunction, whereas high salt directly triggered vascular smooth muscle oxidative stress, poly adenosine diphosphate-ribose polymerase and transient receptor potential melastatin two activation, inflammasome assembly, and interleukin one beta and interleukin eighteen production, linking salt excess to vascular injury and elevated blood pressure (PMID not available for platelet study; PubMed:40312994). Additional support for the clinical relevance of interleukin-driven inflammation comes from observational evidence that latent tuberculosis infection, a condition marked by chronic interleukin-rich inflammatory signaling, is associated with increased incident hypertension [[219]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33263262). Finally, not all interleukin signals are pathogenic in the same direction: impaired interleukin fifteen signaling secondary to bone morphogenetic protein receptor type two loss worsened pulmonary hypertension by reducing natural killer cell homeostasis, showing that loss of protective interleukin circuits can also favor hypertensive vascular disease [[220]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36043416). Overall, the pathway is related to hypertension through several integrated mechanisms, including immune cell activation and polarization, cytokine amplification, endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle migration and remodeling, neuroinflammation, and end-organ injury, making interleukin signaling a biologically coherent and therapeutically relevant framework for understanding hypertension.[[212]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37260032) [[213]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38049579) [[214]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40670501) [[215]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38602915) [[216]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29767573) [[217]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32813135) [[218]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41177181) [[221]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40312994) [[219]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33263262) [[220]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36043416) 

Consistent with these literature-based observations, the enrichment results indicate that this pathway captures a substantial hypertension-relevant functional module. There were 53 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway Signaling by interleukins, indicating that this immune communication program may connect inflammatory signaling with vascular, cerebral, pulmonary, and end-organ pathobiology. This enrichment is biologically coherent because interleukin-mediated signaling regulates endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, oxidative stress, smooth muscle proliferation, tissue remodeling, and cytokine amplification, all of which are central processes in hypertension progression and complication development. Within this 53-protein set, the pathway description highlights several quantitatively important interleukin-centered axes, including interleukin seventeen signaling, interleukin six signaling through glycoprotein one hundred thirty and soluble interleukin six receptor-dependent trans-signaling, interleukin one beta production driven by inflammasome activation, and interleukin fifteen deficiency linked to disrupted natural killer cell homeostasis. Together, these observations support the interpretation that multiple distinct but convergent inflammatory circuits are represented in the enriched protein group. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 53 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for interactive inspection.

![PPI Network](imgs/ddf35fc5-ca6b-4645-8f32-f490b3e80c93.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=6C3747E32BC8AB7D)

To further clarify how this enriched set may relate to hypertension biology, the function enrichment analysis identified several proteins of particular interest. We introduce them in detail below.  
VEGFA stands out as the protein with the most direct and biologically compelling connection to hypertension because its annotated functions converge on endothelial homeostasis, vascular remodeling, and nitric oxide signaling, all of which are core determinants of blood pressure regulation. The described ability to promote endothelial proliferation, migration, and survival indicates an essential role in maintaining vascular integrity, while its regulation of vascular permeability and actin cytoskeletal dynamics suggests direct effects on vessel structure and responsiveness. Particularly relevant to hypertension is the annotation that VEGFA signaling is required for induction of NOS2 and NOS3 and thereby nitric oxide production in endothelial cells. Nitric oxide is a major vasodilator, and impaired endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability is a well-established mechanism contributing to increased vascular tone and elevated blood pressure. In parallel, activation of phosphoinositide three-kinase, protein kinase B, mitogen-activated protein kinase, extracellular signal-regulated kinase, SRC, and focal adhesion kinase pathways links VEGFA to adaptive or maladaptive vascular remodeling, which can influence arterial stiffness and microvascular rarefaction in hypertensive disease. The presence of soluble or decoy receptor isoforms that modulate VEGFA and VEGFC availability further suggests that altered signaling balance could affect lymphangiogenic and vascular responses relevant to fluid handling and pressure control. Overall, this protein appears highly relevant to hypertension because it integrates endothelial signaling, vasodilatory capacity, angiogenesis, and structural vascular adaptation.  

Building on this vascular signaling perspective, the next protein emphasizes the importance of redox control in hypertension.  
SOD2 is highly relevant to hypertension because oxidative stress is one of the principal molecular mechanisms driving endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and abnormal vasoconstriction. By detoxifying superoxide radicals, SOD2 limits the accumulation of reactive oxygen species that would otherwise reduce nitric oxide bioavailability through oxidative inactivation. This is especially important in the vasculature, where excess superoxide promotes impaired endothelium-dependent relaxation, increased vascular tone, and remodeling of resistance arteries, all of which contribute to sustained blood pressure elevation. Given that mitochondrial reactive oxygen species are increasingly recognized as contributors to hypertensive target-organ injury, the protective antioxidant role of SOD2 may also be relevant to cardiac, renal, and vascular damage associated with chronic hypertension. Although the provided annotation is concise, the function described is mechanistically central to hypertension pathogenesis because redox imbalance is tightly linked to both initiation and progression of high blood pressure.
