In parallel with oxidative stress, inflammatory chemokine signaling may provide an additional route through which the enriched protein set intersects with vascular dysfunction.  
CCL5 is of interest in hypertension primarily because its annotated signaling profile implicates inflammatory and calcium-dependent pathways that are highly relevant to vascular dysfunction. Chemokine signaling is increasingly understood to contribute to hypertension through recruitment and activation of immune cells, amplification of vascular inflammation, and promotion of remodeling in the vessel wall and target organs. The noted coupling to guanine nucleotide-binding protein subunit q proteins, inositol trisphosphate generation, and calcium mobilization is particularly notable, because intracellular calcium is a central regulator of vascular smooth muscle contraction and endothelial signaling. In addition, activation of phosphoinositide three-kinase, protein kinase B, and mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways suggests potential effects on cell survival, inflammatory activation, and structural remodeling. Although the annotation emphasizes neuronal survival and possible regulation of insulin secretion, the broader signaling architecture of this receptor is compatible with mechanisms implicated in hypertension, especially the inflammatory-endothelial axis and calcium-sensitive vascular responses. Thus, CCL5 may represent a plausible immunovascular contributor rather than a primary hemodynamic regulator.  

Shifting from inflammatory signaling to cellular stress responses, the following candidate may be more relevant to hypertensive tissue injury than to direct blood pressure regulation.  
CDKN1A is not a classical hypertension gene, but it is potentially relevant because vascular and renal injury in hypertension are strongly influenced by stress-induced cell cycle arrest, senescence, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. The annotated role of CDKN1A in deoxyribonucleic acid damage responses and growth arrest suggests that it may act as a molecular link between hemodynamic stress, oxidative injury, and altered cellular turnover in endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, or renal parenchymal cells. In chronic hypertension, repeated mechanical and oxidative stress can induce deoxyribonucleic acid damage and senescence-like programs, which in turn promote inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular stiffening. CDKN1A-mediated inhibition of proliferation may therefore be protective in some contexts by limiting uncontrolled remodeling, yet detrimental in others by favoring senescence and impaired tissue repair. This duality makes CDKN1A particularly interesting in relation to hypertensive target-organ damage rather than primary blood pressure control. Its functional annotation is supported by specific literature references documenting roles in G2 arrest and cyclin-cyclin-dependent kinase regulation.[[222]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37178686) [[223]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25329316) [[224]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36689330) 

A related but more indirect layer of relevance may arise from metabolic and redox adaptation, which brings attention to TALDO1.  
TALDO1 is potentially relevant to hypertension because pentose phosphate pathway activity is closely tied to cellular redox balance, nucleotide metabolism, and metabolic adaptation under stress. Although TALDO1 does not directly regulate vascular tone, its role in the pentose phosphate pathway suggests an indirect influence on oxidative stress handling and endothelial or renal cell resilience. Metabolic dysfunction and redox imbalance are major contributors to hypertension, particularly in cardiometabolic disease, and enzymes that shape these pathways may affect susceptibility to vascular injury. The annotation that TALDO1 can alter other metabolic pathways through changes in subcellular localization further raises the possibility that it participates in broader stress responses. Therefore, TALDO1 is best considered a secondary or contextual hypertension-related protein, especially in settings where metabolic syndrome, oxidative stress, or endothelial dysfunction are prominent.[[225]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18687684) [[226]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8955144) 

Finally, extending from metabolic and vascular mechanisms to neuroimmune regulation, CRLF1 may represent a more context-dependent candidate.  
CRLF1 has a less direct connection to hypertension than VEGFA or SOD2, but it may still be of interest because neuroimmune mechanisms contribute to blood pressure regulation. Its role in a neurotropic cytokine complex suggests potential relevance to autonomic or sensory neural pathways that influence cardiovascular homeostasis, while its possible immune regulatory function could intersect with inflammatory components of hypertension. However, based on the provided annotation, the evidence is currently more suggestive than definitive. CRLF1 would therefore be considered a lower-priority candidate whose importance may depend on specific disease contexts involving neuroimmune dysregulation rather than core vascular mechanisms of hypertension.

### regulation of blood pressure (GO:0008217) 

Regulation of blood pressure comprises the integrated physiological processes that determine the force exerted by circulating blood on the arterial wall. This pathway is maintained through dynamic interactions among the kidney, vasculature, heart, nervous system, endocrine signals, immune mechanisms, and environmental inputs such as dietary sodium and microbial metabolites. Under normal conditions, blood pressure is stabilized by balancing mechanisms that increase vascular tone, cardiac output, and sodium and water retention against mechanisms that promote vasodilation, natriuresis, and volume reduction. The publications provided suggest that this pathway extends beyond classical hemodynamic control and includes tissue sodium storage, renal tubular sodium transport, endothelial vasoactive mediators, arterial stiffness, autonomic regulation, circadian blood pressure patterning, sex-dependent hormonal modulation, gut microbiota, and immune-inflammatory signaling. In particular, sodium handling by the kidney and extrarenal tissues, including non-osmotic sodium storage in skin and muscle, has emerged as a potentially important determinant of blood pressure homeostasis. Renal sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb through sodium potassium two chloride cotransporter activity also appears to represent a key component of long-term blood pressure control. At the vascular level, endothelial balance between nitric oxide and endothelin one influences vasoconstriction, oxidative stress, inflammation, vascular remodeling, and arterial stiffening. In parallel, the gut microbiota may contribute to blood pressure regulation through production of short-chain fatty acids and other metabolites that act on host receptors, alter immune tone, and influence sympathetic outflow through the gut-brain axis. Taken together, regulation of blood pressure can be viewed as a multi-organ and multi-scale pathway whose disruption may contribute to the initiation, maintenance, and complications of hypertension.  

Building on this physiological framework, the provided literature further indicates how disruption of these coordinated processes may be linked to hypertensive disease states. The literature indicates that hypertension is fundamentally a disease of disordered regulation of blood pressure, arising when the normal balance between pressure-raising and pressure-lowering mechanisms becomes chronically shifted toward vasoconstriction, sodium retention, volume expansion, sympathetic activation, vascular remodeling, and inflammatory signaling. A central theme is abnormal sodium handling: altered sodium and fluid balance promotes hypertension not only through renal retention but also through non-osmotic sodium storage in tissues, which engages immune pathways and contributes to persistent elevation of blood pressure, particularly in salt-sensitive states [[227]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31608291). This renal component is reinforced by evidence that molecular regulation of sodium potassium two chloride cotransporter activity in the thick ascending limb is crucial for sodium chloride reabsorption and long-term blood pressure control, making this transporter an important mechanistic link between the pathway and hypertension [[228]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31313674). Vascular dysfunction represents another major axis connecting this pathway to disease, because increased endothelin one activity together with reduced nitric oxide bioavailability promotes endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, arterial stiffness, and vascular remodeling, all of which elevate peripheral resistance and sustain hypertension [[229]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34575135) [[230]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38214376). The publications also expand the pathway to include gut-derived regulation, showing that gut microbiota composition and its metabolites, especially short-chain fatty acids, influence blood pressure through inflammatory, endocrine, and receptor-mediated mechanisms, while gut-brain communication can amplify sympathetic nervous system activity and neuroinflammation, thereby increasing blood pressure in experimental hypertension [[231]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36674891) [[232]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35912645) [[233]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29118721) [[234]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30930793) [[235]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28264861) [[236]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36153618). In addition, sex-dependent differences in renal sodium handling, vascular biology, hormonal control, endothelin signaling, immune responses, and autonomic regulation may modify susceptibility to hypertension and may help explain differences in disease trajectory and treatment response across the life course [[237]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37477622) [[238]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40931835). Clinical manifestations of impaired blood pressure regulation are further reflected in abnormal blood pressure variability and disturbed day-night blood pressure patterns, which are associated with altered autonomic function and target-organ injury, emphasizing that hypertension is not merely a static elevation in blood pressure but a broader failure of coordinated cardiovascular regulation [[239]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36723481) [[240]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41491847). Collectively, these studies support a close relationship between the pathway of regulation of blood pressure and hypertension, because defects across renal, vascular, neural, immune, microbial, and hormonal components appear to converge on sustained elevation of arterial pressure and its complications.[[227]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31608291) [[228]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31313674) [[229]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34575135) [[230]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38214376) [[231]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36674891) [[232]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35912645) [[233]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29118721) [[234]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30930793) [[235]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28264861) [[236]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36153618) [[237]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37477622) [[238]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40931835) [[239]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36723481) [[240]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41491847) 

This broader disease context is also consistent with the enrichment results obtained for the present protein set. There were 21 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway regulating blood pressure, a complex multi-organ process that integrates renal sodium handling, vascular tone control, cardiac output regulation, autonomic signaling, endocrine modulation, immune-inflammatory activity, tissue sodium storage, circadian variation, sex-dependent hormonal effects, and microbial metabolite signaling. This enrichment is biologically consistent with hypertension because sustained elevation of arterial pressure emerges when the quantitative balance shifts toward greater vasoconstriction, higher sodium and water retention, increased arterial stiffness, enhanced sympathetic drive, and amplified inflammatory signaling, while counter-regulatory processes such as vasodilation, natriuresis, and volume reduction become insufficient. In this context, the identified protein set maps to a pathway in which the kidney, vasculature, heart, nervous system, immune system, and gut collectively determine blood pressure homeostasis, thereby supporting the relevance of all 21 proteins to hypertension pathogenesis and progression. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 21 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network inspection.

![PPI Network](imgs/9cee25a6-4274-4226-ad23-4311acfd4c89.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=9F800ACAF4C79A77)

To further clarify how this enrichment may relate to hypertension biology, the most significant proteins are discussed below in the same functional context. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

ACVRL1 is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to hypertension because it directly regulates endothelial signaling and angiogenesis, two processes central to vascular tone, arterial remodeling, and peripheral resistance. Its dependence on endoglin and SMAD1 places it within the transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein signaling axis, which is well known to influence vascular integrity and endothelial homeostasis. Dysregulation of endothelial growth control can contribute to maladaptive vascular remodeling, rarefaction, and impaired vasodilatory capacity, all of which are mechanistically linked to elevated blood pressure. Moreover, the ACVRL1-endoglin pathway has established relevance to vascular disease states characterized by abnormal vessel structure and hemodynamics, making this protein particularly important when considering hypertension as a disorder of both vascular function and remodeling.  

Consistent with this emphasis on vascular development and endothelial regulation, DLL1 appears to highlight a related but distinct signaling layer. DLL1 stands out strongly because its functions intersect directly with vascular development, arterial specification, angiogenesis, and blood pressure regulation. The Notch pathway is a major determinant of vascular patterning and smooth muscle-endothelial communication, and the description explicitly notes roles in maintaining arterial identity and regulating blood pressure and energy homeostasis. Through its effects on KDR and VEGFA signaling and tip-cell differentiation, DLL1 may influence microvascular architecture and vessel responsiveness, which are relevant to systemic vascular resistance. In addition, Notch signaling has broad effects on tissue remodeling and cell fate decisions in the vasculature, suggesting that altered DLL1 activity could contribute not only to developmental vascular abnormalities but also to adult vascular dysfunction that predisposes to hypertension. Because the provided annotation explicitly connects DLL1 to blood pressure regulation, it is one of the most directly relevant candidates in this dataset.[[241]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11006133) [[242]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11581320) 

Beyond vascular patterning, inflammatory and hemostatic signaling may provide an additional mechanistic bridge to hypertension. F2R is highly relevant to hypertension because it links coagulation, vascular signaling, inflammation, and calcium-dependent cellular responses. Thrombin receptor activation can alter endothelial and vascular cell behavior through intracellular calcium mobilization, a fundamental mechanism in vasomotor regulation and vascular reactivity. Particularly important is the annotation that F2R mediates induction of MCP-1, CCL2, and IL6, inflammatory mediators that are frequently elevated in vascular inflammation and hypertensive target-organ injury. Its roles in platelet activation and vascular development further support a contribution to vascular dysfunction and pro-thrombotic states, both of which commonly accompany hypertension. Thus, F2R may be mechanistically connected to hypertension through inflammatory vascular remodeling, endothelial activation, and altered hemostatic signaling.[[243]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25645137) 

A related extension of this theme is provided by GAS6, which may connect endothelial resilience with thrombotic susceptibility. GAS6 is a notable hypertension-related candidate because it integrates endothelial survival signaling with platelet activation and thrombosis-related pathways. The GAS6 and AXL axis is particularly important in vascular biology, where it can preserve endothelial viability under stress conditions and influence vascular remodeling, inflammation, and thrombotic susceptibility. These functions are relevant to hypertension, which is frequently accompanied by endothelial dysfunction, arterial injury, and increased cardiovascular risk. The annotation highlighting regulation of thrombotic responses and platelet activation further strengthens its relevance, as hypertensive vascular disease often coexists with a pro-thrombotic state. Therefore, GAS6 may contribute to hypertension not necessarily as a primary blood pressure regulator, but as an important modulator of vascular resilience and downstream cardiovascular complications.  

In addition to these endothelial and thrombo-inflammatory factors, proteins linked to structural homeostasis of major effector organs also warrant attention. Although the functional annotation for SCPEP1 is relatively brief, it is still potentially important in hypertension because it implicates two organ systems central to blood pressure control: the vasculature and the kidney. Vascular wall homeostasis is directly related to arterial stiffness, remodeling, and resistance vessel function, whereas kidney homeostasis is fundamental for sodium balance, extracellular fluid volume, and long-term blood pressure regulation. Even in the absence of a detailed mechanistic description, a protein associated with both vascular and renal integrity deserves attention in the context of hypertension, particularly as these are the principal effector organs in hypertensive pathophysiology.  

Finally, oxidative balance provides another plausible layer through which the enriched protein set may influence blood pressure regulation. SOD2 is highly relevant to hypertension because oxidative stress is a well-established driver of endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and impaired nitric oxide bioavailability. By detoxifying mitochondrial superoxide, SOD2 limits reactive oxygen species accumulation that would otherwise promote vasoconstriction, vascular stiffening, and hypertensive end-organ damage. Mitochondrial redox imbalance has been implicated in both the initiation and maintenance of elevated blood pressure, particularly in the vasculature, kidney, and heart. Therefore, SOD2 represents an important protective factor whose reduced activity or increased demand could contribute to the oxidative component of hypertension pathogenesis.

### collagen metabolic process (GO:0032963) 

The collagen metabolic process comprises the synthesis, post-translational modification, assembly, cross-linking, deposition, remodeling, and degradation of collagen, the principal structural protein of the extracellular matrix in connective tissues. Collagen provides tensile strength and mechanical stability to blood vessels, myocardium, and other organs that are critically involved in blood pressure regulation and target-organ injury. This pathway includes intracellular biosynthetic steps such as procollagen production and hydroxylation of proline residues, extracellular fibril formation, and dynamic turnover mediated by proteases and their inhibitors. In vascular and cardiac tissues, balanced collagen metabolism is essential for preserving wall compliance, elasticity, and normal cell-matrix signaling. Disturbance of this balance can lead either to excessive collagen accumulation, which promotes fibrosis and stiffening, or to abnormal collagen proteolysis, which alters mechanotransduction and stimulates maladaptive cellular responses. The publications provided indicate that collagen metabolism is tightly regulated by oxidative stress, inflammation, immune activation, transforming growth factor beta-related and independent profibrotic signaling, aldosterone-related signaling, epigenetic mechanisms, and matrix metalloproteinase activity. Thus, collagen metabolism is not merely a passive structural pathway, but may be considered a central effector of vascular remodeling, myocardial fibrosis, microvascular dysfunction, and altered arterial mechanics.

Against this biological background, the collected literature supports a pathogenic association between dysregulated collagen metabolism and hypertension through vascular fibrosis, arterial stiffening, microvascular remodeling, and cardiac injury. A central theme is that oxidative stress initiates immune and fibrotic responses that increase vascular collagen deposition; in mice with excessive vascular reactive oxygen species production, collagen accumulation in the aorta was accompanied by aortic stiffening, renal dysfunction, and hypertension, and these abnormalities depended on T lymphocyte activation and were prevented by scavenging oxidative products, indicating that collagen deposition is likely to be a mechanistic component rather than a secondary byproduct of elevated pressure alone [[244]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26595812). Consistent with this concept, studies of resistance vessels in essential hypertension showed earlier and more extensive collagen fiber deposition together with oxidative stress and structural remodeling than in physiological aging, supporting the view that hypertension accelerates profibrotic extracellular matrix remodeling [[245]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27802422). Collagen metabolic imbalance in hypertension also involves altered degradation. In early renovascular hypertension, increased matrix metalloproteinase two activity promoted type one collagen proteolysis, which activated focal adhesion kinase signaling and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, thereby contributing to hypertrophic remodeling of the aortic wall; this observation suggests that both excess collagen deposition and abnormal collagen breakdown can drive hypertensive vascular pathology through distinct mechanisms [[246]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37607602). Beyond the systemic vasculature, pulmonary vascular disease provides complementary evidence that collagen metabolism is directly linked to hypertensive remodeling: neural precursor cell expressed developmentally down-regulated nine promoted collagen type three alpha one expression, increased endothelial stiffness, and enhanced collagen one and collagen three accumulation in pulmonary vascular cells, while its inhibition prevented fibrotic remodeling and pulmonary arterial hypertension in vivo [[247]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29899023). Similarly, right ventricular fibroblasts in experimental pulmonary arterial hypertension exhibited a persistent metabolic program that increased collagen production and fibrosis, and pharmacological reversal of this program reduced fibrosis and improved function, further connecting collagen synthesis to hypertensive end-organ damage [[248]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32216531). Cardiac studies in systemic hypertension also reinforce this relationship, as inhibition of deoxyribonucleic acid methylation reduced collagen one and collagen three expression, myocardial fibrosis, and hypertrophy in spontaneously hypertensive rats, indicating that epigenetic control of collagen metabolism contributes to pressure-induced cardiac remodeling [[249]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26130616). Clinical and translational observations align with these experimental findings: patients with arterial hypertension exhibit increased myocardial interstitial collagen and elevated circulating markers of collagen formation and fibrosis, which can be attenuated by antihypertensive therapy with antifibrotic properties [[250]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32145168), while recent reviews identify excessive collagen deposition as a core feature of hypertensive microvascular dysfunction that increases vascular resistance and promotes injury in the heart, kidney, brain, and retina [[251]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39769057). Collectively, these studies indicate that the collagen metabolic process is fundamentally involved in hypertension because it translates oxidative, inflammatory, hormonal, metabolic, and mechanical stress into structural remodeling of vessels and myocardium, thereby increasing stiffness, impairing vasodilation, promoting maladaptive cell proliferation, and sustaining target-organ damage.[[244]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26595812) [[245]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27802422) [[246]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37607602) [[247]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29899023) [[248]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32216531) [[249]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26130616) [[250]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32145168) [[251]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39769057) 

Building on this literature-based context, the enrichment result provides a quantitative indication that collagen-related molecular programs may be substantially represented in the hypertension-associated protein set. There were 18 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the collagen metabolic process pathway, indicating a quantitatively substantial convergence of disease-related molecular signals on extracellular matrix regulation, collagen synthesis, post-translational modification, fibril assembly, cross-linking, deposition, remodeling, and degradation. This enrichment is biologically important because collagen is the principal structural protein of connective tissues and is a major determinant of vascular wall tensile strength, myocardial mechanical stability, arterial compliance, and cell-matrix signaling, all of which are directly relevant to blood pressure regulation and hypertension-mediated target-organ injury. In hypertension, even modest shifts in the balance between collagen production and collagen degradation can produce large cumulative effects on tissue architecture, leading to increased vascular stiffness, myocardial fibrosis, impaired microvascular function, and maladaptive mechanotransduction. The identification of 18 proteins within this pathway therefore supports the interpretation that collagen metabolism is not a peripheral feature of hypertension, but rather a central disease-associated process shaped by oxidative stress, inflammation, immune activation, transforming growth factor beta-related and independent profibrotic signaling, aldosterone-related signaling, epigenetic regulation, and matrix metalloproteinase-dependent turnover.

To further contextualize these 18 proteins, the interaction network offers a complementary view of how these molecules may be functionally connected within the broader collagen remodeling landscape. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 18 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and further interaction-based interpretation.

![PPI Network](imgs/0780372e-357b-41fd-9806-1b72dff86438.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=03EB4EA58A271B7F)

With this network-level overview in place, it is useful to consider individual proteins that emerged from the function enrichment analysis and to discuss their possible relevance in a cautious, evidence-based manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

MMP8 stands out as the protein with the clearest potential relevance to hypertension because its collagenolytic activity directly implicates extracellular matrix remodeling. By degrading fibrillar collagens, MMP8 may influence the structural integrity and turnover of the vascular wall, a process that is highly relevant to hypertension, where arterial stiffening, fibrosis, and maladaptive remodeling are central pathophysiological features. Altered collagen balance in resistance arteries and large vessels contributes to increased vascular stiffness and elevated peripheral resistance, both of which promote blood pressure elevation. Therefore, proteins such as MMP8 that regulate collagen degradation may participate in either adaptive remodeling or pathological matrix disruption, depending on context. Although no citation was provided in the input for this function, the biological role itself supports MMP8 as a plausible contributor to hypertension-associated vascular remodeling.

In a related but distinct way, VSIR is notable because it links two mechanisms increasingly recognized in hypertension: immune dysregulation and matrix remodeling. Its reported role as an immunoregulatory receptor that inhibits T-cell responses suggests potential relevance to the inflammatory component of hypertension, as activated T cells and low-grade vascular inflammation are known to contribute to endothelial dysfunction, vascular injury, and sustained blood pressure elevation. In this context, VSIR could influence disease susceptibility or progression by modulating the magnitude of adaptive immune activation. In addition, the reported ability of VSIR to stimulate MMP14-mediated MMP2 activation provides a second mechanistic connection to hypertension, since MMP2 is implicated in vascular extracellular matrix turnover, arterial remodeling, and fibrosis. These combined immune and proteolytic functions make VSIR particularly interesting as a candidate regulator at the intersection of inflammation and structural vascular change in hypertensive disease. The BMP4-related annotation may also be relevant indirectly, because BMP signaling has recognized roles in vascular biology, although the strongest hypertension-related implications here derive from T-cell inhibition and MMP2 pathway activation.[[252]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24691993) [[253]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20666777) 

By contrast, PRSS2 does not stand out in the present dataset because no functional annotation was provided from which to infer a meaningful connection to hypertension. Without a defined role in vascular biology, inflammation, extracellular matrix regulation, renal sodium handling, or neurohormonal signaling, its relevance to hypertension cannot be evaluated on the basis of the supplied information alone.

### Viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (KEGG:04061) 

The pathway entitled viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor describes a host pathogen interface in which viral proteins directly or indirectly engage cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, or their cognate receptors, thereby reshaping immune signaling, leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation, and tissue injury. In respiratory viral infection, this pathway is especially relevant because viral surface or accessory proteins can alter receptor availability, stimulate protease dependent shedding of membrane receptors, amplify proinflammatory transcriptional programs, and disturb the balance between antiviral defense and injurious inflammation. A central example in the cited literature is the interaction between severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two spike protein and angiotensin converting enzyme two, which is not itself a cytokine receptor but functionally intersects with cytokine networks by shifting the renin angiotensin system toward angiotensin two driven inflammation, oxidative stress, vasoconstriction, and fibrosis. This shift promotes downstream induction of inflammatory mediators such as interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin one, chemokine ligand three, chemokine ligand four, chemokine ligand two, and their receptors, while also involving disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain containing protein seventeen mediated shedding of angiotensin converting enzyme two and interleukin six receptor. The pathway therefore links viral entry biology with cytokine storm, endothelial dysfunction, vascular permeability, coagulation, and organ damage. In the context of hypertension, this pathway is particularly important because hypertension is characterized by chronic low grade vascular inflammation, endothelial stress, altered renin angiotensin system signaling, and heightened cytokine responsiveness, all of which can prime tissues and immune cells for exaggerated responses when viral proteins perturb cytokine and cytokine receptor signaling.

Building on this mechanistic framework, the cited studies collectively suggest that this pathway may be related to hypertension because hypertensive individuals appear to enter viral infection with a pre-existing inflammatory and renin angiotensin system imbalance that magnifies the consequences of viral protein driven cytokine and cytokine receptor perturbation. Clinical and single cell data showed that, in coronavirus disease 2019, hypertension was associated with delayed viral clearance and exaggerated airway hyperinflammation, with macrophages and neutrophils displaying increased expression of chemokine ligand three, chemokine ligand four, and chemokine receptor one, indicating that hypertensive immune cells are predisposed to stronger cytokine and chemokine signaling after viral challenge [[254]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33361824). Multiple reviews further explain that severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two binding to angiotensin converting enzyme two reduces the protective angiotensin converting enzyme two axis and favors angiotensin two signaling through angiotensin receptor type one, which drives inflammation, reactive oxygen species generation, vascular permeability, remodeling, and cytokine excess; this mechanism is especially relevant in hypertension because hypertension already involves dysregulation of this hormonal and inflammatory network [[255]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32338224) [[256]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33195436) [[257]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32719447). Additional work proposes that the interplay among angiotensin converting enzyme two, transmembrane protease serine two, and disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain containing protein seventeen may intensify shedding of angiotensin converting enzyme two and interleukin six receptor, thereby amplifying tumor necrosis factor and interleukin six linked inflammatory cascades in patients with hypertension and other cardiometabolic disorders [[258]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33117379). The broader hypertension literature supports the biological plausibility of this connection, because vascular injury in hypertension is sustained by cytokine and growth factor networks that activate endothelial cells, leukocyte recruitment, and maladaptive repair responses, and antihypertensive interventions with anti-inflammatory effects can modulate genes enriched in cytokine interaction pathways, including chemokine ligand two and fos proto-oncogene, in endothelial cells [[259]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1456874) [[260]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39517176). Taken together, the pathway appears to be linked to hypertension not because viral proteins cause primary hypertension, but because hypertension may create a cytokine sensitive vascular and immune environment in which viral manipulation of cytokines and cytokine receptors more readily triggers hyperinflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and severe organ injury.[[254]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33361824) [[255]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32338224) [[256]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33195436) [[257]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32719447) [[258]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33117379) [[259]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1456874) [[260]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39517176) 

Consistent with the literature-based rationale above, the enrichment results provide a quantitative layer of support for the relevance of this pathway to hypertension. There were 35 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway entitled viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, indicating a substantial convergence between hypertension-related molecular alterations and host inflammatory signaling mechanisms that are perturbed during viral infection. This enrichment is biologically notable because hypertension is strongly linked to chronic vascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, altered angiotensin signaling, oxidative stress, and increased sensitivity to inflammatory mediators, all of which are highly consistent with the functional scope of this pathway. The pathway description further supports this interpretation by highlighting interactions that connect viral proteins with cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and their receptors, while also linking severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two spike protein engagement with angiotensin converting enzyme two to downstream increases in angiotensin two driven inflammation, vasoconstriction, fibrosis, endothelial activation, vascular permeability, coagulation, and tissue injury. Within this framework, the enrichment of 35 proteins suggests that a relatively broad protein set, rather than an isolated molecular event, contributes to the interface between hypertension and dysregulated immune signaling, especially through mediators such as interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin one, chemokine ligand three, chemokine ligand four, and chemokine ligand two, together with receptor shedding processes involving disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain containing protein seventeen. Collectively, the presence of 35 enriched proteins supports the interpretation that this pathway captures a quantitatively substantial and mechanistically coherent inflammatory axis relevant to hypertension.

To further contextualize this enriched protein set, the network visualization below illustrates how these 35 proteins may be interconnected at the protein-protein interaction level, thereby providing a complementary systems-level view of the pathway enrichment result. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 35 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link below.

![PPI Network](imgs/ba8e3a25-888f-49c9-8c56-55fdb29e00c0.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=EBA629DA5CD959CA)

With this network context in place, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance in a hypertension-related setting. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
CCL5 is notable in the context of hypertension because it is a pro-inflammatory chemokine whose downstream signaling profile is highly relevant to vascular biology, neurohumoral regulation, and cardiometabolic disease. Its ability to activate G protein-dependent calcium signaling suggests potential effects on leukocyte activation, endothelial behavior, and vascular tone-related inflammatory responses. More importantly, the linked PI3K-AKT-MAPK pathways are central to cell survival, vascular remodeling, and inflammatory activation, all of which contribute to the development and progression of hypertension and hypertensive end-organ damage. The reported connection to neuron survival may also be relevant because neuroimmune interactions and autonomic dysregulation are increasingly recognized as contributors to blood pressure elevation. In addition, the observation that CCL5 signaling may regulate insulin secretion connects this axis to metabolic dysfunction, which frequently coexists with hypertension and amplifies cardiovascular risk. Thus, although the provided annotation emphasizes receptor-mediated signaling rather than a direct hypertensive phenotype, CCL5 stands out as a plausible contributor to hypertension through inflammation-driven vascular dysfunction, remodeling, neuroimmune signaling, and metabolic crosstalk.
